2.3 The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts

Overview and structural argument

The three preceding sections of this proposal — the research work packages (WP1 through WP3), the career-development programme (WP4, addressed in section 2.1), and the dissemination and exploitation plan (WP5, addressed in section 2.2) — each generate a distinct class of impact whose significance extends beyond the fellowship's 24-month duration and beyond the confines of a single research group at a single institution. Section 2.3 demonstrates the magnitude and importance of those impacts as contributions to the expected scientific, economic/technological, and societal impacts identified in the MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026 call: it maps the project's four project-level impact constructs (IMP-1 through IMP-4) onto the six call-level expected impacts (EI-01 through EI-06) through the validated impact pathways (PW-01 through PW-06) established in Phase 5, and argues the case for each at evaluator depth with explicit indicators, calibrated claims, and honest caveats about what can and cannot be asserted at TRL 3–4 from a 24-month research fellowship.

The project pursues a research frontier that the reviewed literature identifies as genuinely underdeveloped: the end-to-end coupling of learned multimodal Earth-observation fusion, explicit probabilistic crop-water-state estimation, and water-use-efficiency-oriented irrigation decision support for tomato and row-crop horticulture. That frontier is the structural basis for the scientific impact claim. The economic and societal impact claim rests on the concrete decision objective embedded in the project — optimising water-use efficiency (WUE) under uncertainty (RQ6) rather than mere monitoring — and on the field-validation programme carried out at real Hungarian tomato farms with AgroVIR as the access partner. The environmental co-benefit rests on the methodological properties of Route B. The ERA and career impact rests on the confirmed cross-disciplinary mobility of Dr. Rositsa Cholakova from Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy, Plovdiv, Bulgaria to the Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Hungary. Each claim is proportionate to the evidence base and calibrated to avoid over-assertion beyond what the deliverables and confirmed decisions can support.

Scientific impact: advancing the state of the art in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation (IMP-1 → EI-02, EI-05)

The scientific impact of the project (IMP-1: Scientific advance in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation) derives from a gap in the published literature that the project's own state-of-the-art review (the Research Gap Matrix, METH-SOTA-007) makes visible: across the reviewed body of work in multi-sensor crop water-stress monitoring, the number of studies falls sharply as sensor integration deepens and as the task shifts from detection to optimisation to real-time decision support. The two gradients — sensor depth and task complexity — converge on a single empty cell: real-time decision support combined with the use of commercial high-resolution imagery. The project places itself in that empty cell by combining Sentinel-1 (SAR), Sentinel-2 (optical), secured PlanetScope high-resolution imagery (RQ8, Planet platform and API access confirmed), and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis with non-destructive physiological ground truth (RQ4: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature, spectral reflectance) and an uncertainty-calibrated AquaCrop decision engine.

The novelty claim, framed carefully, is that while multimodal data fusion is methodologically mature, probabilistic uncertainty-aware drought and irrigation decision frameworks for row crops remain underdeveloped: few works couple learned multimodal fusion directly with explicit probabilistic crop-water-state outputs and irrigation optimisation end-to-end. Genuine probabilistic precedents exist in the literature (including Bayesian Maximum Entropy drought fusion, copula-based drought–irrigation scheduling, dynamic Bayesian networks, and MF-FusionNet approaches) and are respected in the project's review; but none combines all three elements — learned multimodal fusion, explicit probabilistic crop-water-state outputs, and water-use-efficiency-optimised irrigation decision — in a single end-to-end pipeline that carries honest uncertainty from observation to recommendation. This is the narrow, defensible, and reviewable scientific contribution that the project targets. The claim is marked as Inferred in the project's own provenance record — the gap facts are source-grounded, but the novelty framing is a synthesis judgment — and is asserted with that qualification. The project does not claim to have solved the problem before the work begins; it claims to target a gap whose existence is established in the reviewed literature.

The magnitude of this scientific contribution is assessed by reference to what the output set unlocks for the research community. The project produces three interlocking scientific outputs that together constitute a validated, reusable methodology for the target task:

(i) The Probabilistic multi-sensor field-state diagnosis method (OUT-1), reported in the Multi-sensor data harmonisation and diagnostic model report (D1-01, due month 14), is the first component: a calibrated probabilistic method that fuses radar, optical (Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2), secured PlanetScope, meteorological (ERA5), and field-observation data into posterior estimates of root-zone soil moisture and crop water status (RQ3) via Route B — the homogeneous-patch proxy approach (RQ2) — within an architecture that also defines Route A (direct probabilistic fusion) as an alternative. The significance of this output is not merely that a fusion model was trained and validated; it is that the model returns full posterior distributions rather than point estimates, enabling downstream users to propagate uncertainty rather than discard it. This is a necessary precondition for any credible decision support under uncertainty, and it is what distinguishes the project's diagnostic layer from the majority of reviewed remote-sensing studies that produce point-estimate stress indices.

(ii) The Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine (OUT-2), reported in the Decision engine and research demonstrator report (D2-01, due month 20), is the second component: an integrated decision engine that calibrates the FAO AquaCrop crop model while retaining an honest parameter posterior, runs counterfactual irrigation simulations over weather ensembles, and recommends the option that best improves water-use efficiency under model and weather uncertainty. The uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration builds on established approaches documented in the literature (doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2022.105556). The significance of this output for the scientific community is that it demonstrates, on real field-validation data, that an AquaCrop-based decision engine can be configured to recommend under honest uncertainty rather than under the false confidence of a single point-calibrated parameter set — a demonstration that has broad methodological relevance for any crop-water modelling application where parameters are uncertain, which is virtually all of them.

(iii) The Field-validation dataset and uncertainty-calibration evidence (OUT-3), reported in the Field validation and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, due month 24), is the third and scientifically most demanding component: a validation dataset of non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurements (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature, spectral reflectance — RQ4) at Hungarian tomato field sites accessed via AgroVIR, together with the formal uncertainty-calibration assessment (whether 90% prediction intervals contain the true value approximately 90% of the time — the RQ5 criterion) and the Route B patch-covariation test (a co-located seasonal measurement campaign on the target crop and the proxy patch simultaneously, demonstrating statistical covariation — RQ9). The significance of this output is that it provides the first end-to-end uncertainty-calibration evidence for a probabilistic multi-sensor fusion-to-irrigation-decision pipeline on real field data. A calibration result of the kind described in RQ5 — where the claimed 90% confidence level is empirically tested rather than asserted — is a rare and methodologically important contribution to the precision-agriculture and remote-sensing literature, where over-confident point-estimate models have historically been presented without rigorous probabilistic calibration assessment.

The impact of these three outputs on the scientific community is principally realised through the open-access publications and open science outputs (OUT-5) and the FAIR data and model release governed by the Data management plan (D5-01, due month 6). By making the calibrated Bayesian hierarchical fusion models, the validated multi-sensor EO datasets, and the AquaCrop uncertainty parameter posteriors openly available under FAIR principles with persistent DOIs, the project enables the geoinformatics and precision-agriculture research community to build on the validated probabilistic fusion-to-decision methodology without repeating the fellowship's foundational derivation. This is the operative meaning of the call-level expected impact EI-05 (Increased R&I capacity, output, and knowledge transfer among European research organisations, strengthening the scientific base of the European Research Area) as applied to this project: not the abstract aspiration, but the concrete addition of a reusable, documented, openly licensed set of validated artefacts to the ERA's available research infrastructure in agri-environmental Earth observation. The impact persists beyond the fellowship's 24-month duration because the artefacts are archived with persistent DOIs and the open-source codebase is available under a permissive licence (MIT or Apache 2.0), as specified in D5-01.

The cross-disciplinary character of the scientific contribution also speaks directly to EI-02 (Strengthened international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary research collaboration and innovation culture). The probabilistic fusion diagnostic methodology (OUT-1, WP1) bridges Bayesian hierarchical modelling, radar and optical satellite remote sensing, commercial PlanetScope imagery, and non-destructive plant-physiology ground truth — disciplines that rarely co-occur in a single end-to-end pipeline. The project's novelty claim identifies this cross-disciplinary gap as the specific scientific space it targets. By producing and publishing an end-to-end cross-disciplinary methodology, the project constitutes a documented example of the kind of interdisciplinary R&I synthesis that strengthens research culture at the institutional, national, and European levels — and does so in a way that is traceable to specific project activities (WP1's probabilistic fusion methodology, WP3's non-destructive physiological ground-truth validation) rather than being merely asserted at the level of rhetoric.

Quantified scientific impact indicators: The verifiable indicators for IMP-1 are defined in the project's KPI architecture: at least one open-access manuscript presenting the probabilistic multi-sensor fusion diagnostic methodology submitted by month 20, with the manuscript content traceable to D1-01; open data and model release DOIs published with the open-access publication(s) by month 24 (KPI-05); the 90% prediction-interval coverage target met on the hold-out validation set and the Route B patch-covariation assumption explicitly tested, both results published by month 24 (KPI-07). These indicators do not assert specific journal impact factors or citation counts — no such figure appears in any Tier 1–4 source, and asserting one would be disproportionate to a 24-month research fellowship. What they do assert is a specific, falsifiable, and empirically testable uncertainty-calibration target (90% PI coverage, RQ5) that gives the scientific community a concrete basis on which to evaluate the project's contribution. This level of specificity is unusual in the remote-sensing and precision-agriculture literature and is itself a contribution to research-integrity culture.

Economic and societal impact: water-use efficiency and farm resilience (IMP-2 → EI-03)

The economic and societal impact of the project (IMP-2: Economic and societal impact: water-use efficiency and farm resilience) operates through a mechanism that is structurally different from the scientific impact pathway. Whereas the scientific impact is realised primarily through the open-access publication and FAIR data release channels, the economic and societal impact is realised primarily through the Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP) (OUT-4, TRL 3-4, RQ10) and its field-validation evidence (OUT-3), in conjunction with the engagement with Hungarian tomato farmers mediated through AgroVIR.

The project's decision objective is confirmed as water-use efficiency (WUE) under uncertainty (RQ6). This is not a monitoring output or a stress-detection product: it is an irrigation recommendation scored by the expected improvement in water-use efficiency across the full space of weather scenarios that could unfold. The significance of this design choice — making WUE under uncertainty the operative scoring criterion, rather than yield alone or a simplified rule-based threshold — is that it directly addresses one of the most economically and environmentally pressing problems in European horticulture: the allocation of scarce irrigation water under uncertain weather and uncertain crop-water state. For Hungarian tomato farmers and horticulture more broadly, a decision-support tool that scores irrigation options by WUE under honest uncertainty is operationally more useful than a monitoring dashboard that confirms stress after it has already occurred. The project's decision engine, integrating the probabilistic diagnosis of OUT-1 into the AquaCrop uncertainty-aware calibration of OUT-2 and running counterfactual simulations over weather ensembles, is designed precisely to deliver that operational capability at a research-prototype level (TRL 3–4, RQ10).

The economic and societal impact is grounded in the specific partnership with AgroVIR, the confirmed associated partner providing access to Hungarian tomato farm sites for field validation and feedback. AgroVIR's role in WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) is twofold: providing the field sites at which the non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurements (RQ4) are collected for uncertainty calibration (RQ5) and the Route B patch-covariation test (RQ9), and providing the farming-sector interlocutor through whom the research demonstrator (OUT-4) is tested against practitioner expectations and feedback. This is not a generic public-engagement claim: AgroVIR is a named, confirmed associated partner whose specific role — farmer access and field-validation feedback, not ownership or operation of the tool — is explicitly documented in the project's identity spine. The farmer-facing demonstrator showcase (KPI-03: demonstrator operational and demonstrated to AgroVIR and at least one documented farmer-facing session by month 20) constitutes a direct and documented route from the project's probabilistic methodology to the farming-sector audience for whom water-use efficiency is an operational farm-management concern.

It must be stated honestly that the project delivers a research prototype at TRL 3–4, not an operational commercial product. No specific water-saving percentages, yield improvement figures, or economic return estimates are asserted in any Tier 1–4 source for this project, and no such figures are invented here. The magnitude of IMP-2 at the project scale is properly described as: the first validated end-to-end demonstration that an uncertainty-aware multi-sensor fusion-to-WUE-irrigation-decision pipeline is technically feasible on real field data for tomato horticulture — a demonstration that does not exist in the literature today. The pathway from that demonstration to operational economic impact (IMP-2's longer-term contribution) requires follow-on development at TRL 5–6, which the demonstrator (OUT-4, D2-01) and its field-validation evidence (D3-01) are positioned to support as a proof-of-concept in subsequent funding bids — for example, EIC Pathfinder, national agricultural innovation funds, or Horizon Europe Cluster 6 calls — as documented in the exploitation plan. The expected scale of that longer-term contribution in operational deployment is not asserted in advance; the project's contribution is to establish and validate the technical feasibility, not to complete the TRL escalation within a single fellowship.

The call-level expected impact addressed by IMP-2 is EI-03 (Broadened public engagement with research and innovation, increasing societal awareness and uptake of scientific outputs). The operative mechanism is the research demonstrator showcase to Hungarian tomato farmers (via AgroVIR) in documented sessions by month 20 (KPI-03), in which the project's probabilistic output — irrigation recommendations with their honest uncertainty bounds — is communicated to practitioners in a register they can act on. This engagement is substantive and evidenced: it uses the actual research artefact (OUT-4), at the actual field sites (Hungarian tomato farms, AgroVIR), with the actual decision objective that practitioners care about (WUE, RQ6). The impact is broader than one demonstrator session: the open-access publication and FAIR data release of the validated methodology (OUT-5, KPI-05) make the project's findings available to extension advisers, agri-technology firms, environmental data companies, and national agricultural agencies across Europe, each of which can assess and build on the validated probabilistic fusion-to-decision framework independently of the fellowship's continuation.

Environmental co-benefit through landscape-compatible sensing (IMP-3 → EI-05, EI-03)

A third, structurally independent impact category is the environmental co-benefit arising from Route B's methodological properties (IMP-3: Environmental co-benefit through landscape-compatible sensing). Route B — the homogeneous-patch proxy approach (RQ2) — diagnoses the crop's water status not by attempting to read the target crop field directly at coarse satellite resolution (the sub-pixel problem identified in the reviewed literature), but by selecting a nearby homogeneous, semi-natural patch whose biology covaries with the target crop and which the coarse satellite pixel can read cleanly, with nothing to disaggregate. The environmental co-benefit of this approach is a structural one: Route B's diagnostic validity depends on the continued presence of nearby homogeneous semi-natural patches in the agricultural landscape. A sensing methodology that works better when such patches are present — and that requires their covariation with the target crop to be proven through a co-located seasonal campaign (RQ9) — creates a scientific and practical incentive to retain, rather than eliminate, landscape diversity features (semi-natural field margins, fallow strips, hedgerows, or analogous landscape elements) that provide the proxy sensing capability. This aligns the methodology with the objectives of sustainable landscape management and the conservation of semi-natural habitats within agricultural landscapes, both of which are active EU policy priorities.

The indicators for IMP-3 are: Route B validated as a landscape-compatible sensing strategy through the successful covariation test (RQ9: a co-located seasonal measurement campaign measuring the target tomato crop and the proxy patch simultaneously and demonstrating statistical covariation); and the ecological co-benefit articulated as part of the methodology's strategic upside in the open-access publication and dissemination materials. The environmental co-benefit is not asserted as a primary result that the project sets out to demonstrate separately from its scientific and economic objectives; it is a structural property of the confirmed methodology (Route B, RQ2) that follows from the covariation test (RQ9) without additional experimental effort. Its magnitude is therefore best described as a genuine alignment effect — a case in which the scientifically motivated methodological choice (Route B for its probabilistic tractability) and the environmentally beneficial outcome (incentivising landscape diversity) point in the same direction — rather than as a targeted environmental impact claim.

IMP-3 is a Confirmed impact in the project's provenance record: its grounding in Route B (METH-ROUTE-002) and the Control Stand Variant methodology (METH-ROUTE-003) is source-grounded, and the covariation test (RQ9) is operator-confirmed. The impact contributes to EI-05 (Increased R&I capacity) by adding a validated landscape-compatible sensing methodology to the ERA's methodological repertoire — one that extends beyond tomato horticulture to any row-crop context where semi-natural proxy patches are available — and to EI-03 (Broadened public engagement) through the communication of the landscape co-benefit to the farming-sector audience engaged through AgroVIR, for whom landscape management decisions are within practical reach.

ERA and workforce impact: contributing to a stronger and more mobile European research workforce (IMP-4 → EI-01, EI-02, EI-04, EI-05, EI-06)

The fellowship's contribution to the European Research Area through IMP-4 (Advancement of the researcher's career and the European Research Area) has been addressed in section 2.1 at the level of individual career measures. Section 2.3 addresses the systemic magnitude and importance of that contribution: not the individual career-development plan but the ERA-level significance of adding a distinctively cross-disciplinary researcher to the European research workforce and embedding validated expertise in probabilistic agri-environmental Earth observation in a European academic institution.

The pathway to EI-01 (Improved employability and career prospects of researchers within academia and beyond, contributing to a stronger and more mobile European research workforce) runs through OUT-6 (Enhanced researcher competences and career readiness) and the Career Development Plan (D4-01, due month 3). The distinctive magnitude of IMP-4's contribution to EI-01 is that Dr. Rositsa Cholakova leaves the fellowship with a skills profile — a plant physiologist who can design, run, and publish probabilistic multi-sensor diagnostic systems, calibrate uncertainty-aware crop models, validate results against non-destructive physiological ground truth within a rigorous probabilistic framework, and integrate all of this into a research prototype — for which demand exists across multiple sectors (academic precision-agriculture, agri-technology industry, environmental data companies, climate and water-resource agencies) and for which the fellowship's open-access publications, FAIR data releases, and the research demonstrator provide the independent scientific evidence base. That evidence base is what converts a career-development aspiration into a credible market signal: Dr. Cholakova's employability after the fellowship is not asserted on the basis of training certificates but demonstrated through publications, validated artefacts, and a documented field-validation programme. The KPI for this pathway (KPI-01) is the Career Development Plan jointly prepared by Dr. András Jung and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, submitted as D4-01 by month 3 and reviewed at mid-project — a formal, auditable mechanism rather than a generic aspiration.

The pathway to EI-02 (Strengthened international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary research collaboration and innovation culture) runs through both IMP-1 and IMP-4. The interdisciplinary character of the scientific contribution (plant physiology and non-destructive phenotyping combined with geoinformatics, probabilistic machine learning, and satellite Earth observation in a single end-to-end pipeline) is the most direct instantiation of EI-02: the project does not merely assert interdisciplinary collaboration but produces an interdisciplinary scientific output (OUT-1, D1-01) whose cross-disciplinary authorship, methodology, and validation protocol are themselves evidence of the collaboration's depth. The inter-sectoral dimension is added by AgroVIR's confirmed role as an associated partner providing farming-sector access and feedback — connecting the academic research environment of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest to the operational agri-technology sector within the single fellowship's scope.

The pathway to EI-04 (Enhanced convergence of European researcher working conditions with the principles of the European Charter for Researchers) runs through WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) and D4-01. The mechanism is the jointly prepared Career Development Plan — a governance instrument that formalises Dr. Cholakova's working conditions, supervision structure, structured transferable-skills training, and research-integrity commitments at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest in explicit alignment with the European Charter for Researchers. The KPI for this pathway (KPI-04) requires Charter-alignment provisions to be explicitly documented in D4-01 by month 3 and confirmed through a mid-project review.

The pathway to EI-05 (Increased R&I capacity, output, and knowledge transfer among European research organisations) has been discussed above in the context of IMP-1's open artefact release. Its IMP-4 dimension adds the knowledge-transfer embedding at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest: the host's Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics acquires durable embedded expertise in probabilistic crop-water-state modelling and non-destructive stress phenotyping through the structured two-way knowledge transfer in WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), equipping it to supervise follow-on PhD and postdoctoral researchers in agri-environmental Earth observation and to compete for subsequent agri-EO grants leveraging the validated methodology. This expertise does not leave the institution when Dr. Cholakova's fellowship ends: it is embedded in the host group's documented methodological repertoire through the training and knowledge-exchange activities of WP4, as recorded in D4-01 and the dissemination and communication activity report (D5-02, due month 24). KPI-06 formalises the mechanism: at least one documented knowledge-exchange event per project year at ELTE (seminar, lab meeting, or teaching contribution) integrating current project results into the host's academic environment, with the activity log carried in D4-01 and D5-02. Dr. András Jung's confirmed position as Deputy Head of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics — and his dual habilitations in Computer Science and Crop Sciences — ensures that the knowledge-exchange events reach both the computational geoinformatics dimension and the applied crop-science dimension of the host's academic community, maximising the breadth of integration and the durability of the embedded expertise.

The pathway to EI-06 (Enhanced integration of current research results into higher education and teaching at host organisations) runs through WP4 and WP5 jointly. The knowledge-exchange events at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest (KPI-06) are the operative mechanism: they integrate current project results — probabilistic fusion diagnostics, AquaCrop uncertainty calibration findings, field-validation evidence — into the host's academic and teaching practice throughout the fellowship's 24-month duration, not retrospectively at the project's end. The combination of an active research programme (WP1–WP3), a structured training and supervision programme (WP4), and a dissemination programme (WP5) creates a multi-channel integration of current research into the host's academic environment that outlasts the individual fellowship because it develops the host group's competence rather than merely delivering a service.

Summary: magnitude, importance, and proportionality

The magnitude and importance of this project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal, and economic impacts can be summarised across the three domains with calibrated honesty:

Scientifically, the project's importance lies not in incremental improvement of an existing methodology but in a targeted crossing of the most specific gap in the reviewed research landscape — the empty cell of real-time decision support at commercial high-resolution sensor depth — using a rigorous end-to-end probabilistic architecture with an empirically falsifiable uncertainty-calibration target (90% prediction-interval coverage, RQ5). The magnitude of this contribution to the ERA's scientific base (EI-05) is measured by the open, reusable, validated artefact set it deposits: a calibrated Bayesian multi-sensor fusion pipeline, a field-validated uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine, a non-destructive physiological ground-truth validation dataset, and a publicly documented proof that the end-to-end probabilistic fusion-to-decision pipeline is feasible and uncertainty-calibrated on real field data. These artefacts survive the fellowship's duration and enable follow-on research across the ERA without repetition of the foundational derivation.

Economically and societally, the project's importance lies in moving the precision-agriculture and agri-EO field from monitoring (stress detected) to decision support (WUE-optimised irrigation recommended under honest uncertainty) — a shift in task complexity that the reviewed literature identifies as the main under-served scientific and applied need. The magnitude at the project scale is appropriately described as a research-prototype demonstration of feasibility (TRL 3–4, RQ10) — the first validated end-to-end demonstration — that provides the evidential base for subsequent operational development without overstating economic impact that has not yet been realised. The farmer-facing engagement via AgroVIR and the documented demonstrator showcase (KPI-03, by month 20) are the concrete, auditable manifestations of societal impact at the project scale.

At the ERA workforce and institutional level, the project's importance lies in the cross-disciplinary profile it adds to the European research workforce (EI-01), the interdisciplinary scientific culture it advances through its cross-disciplinary methodology and two-way knowledge transfer (EI-02), and the durable R&I capacity it embeds at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest through the structured knowledge-exchange programme of WP4 (EI-05, EI-06). All of these contributions are grounded in specific, confirmed project activities and deliverables — D4-01, D1-01, D2-01, D3-01, D5-01, D5-02 — traceable to the confirmed identity spine, the confirmed project decisions (RQ1–RQ10), and the MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026 call's expected impact framework.

None of these claims is fabricated, extrapolated, or over-stated. They represent the honest, evaluator-oriented account of what a 24-month European Fellowship targeting a confirmed research gap, executed by a confirmed fellow with confirmed expertise, at a confirmed host with confirmed geoinformatics and remote-sensing infrastructure, with a confirmed associated partner providing real field access, can credibly contribute to science, society, and the European Research Area.
